A year after the moon landing, US senator Gaylord Nelson (1916-2005) proposed the first Earth Day on 22 April 1970. The day was marked by a national environment teach-in led by schools, colleges, universities and community groups.
In the USA, public concern for the environment first peaked around the first Earth Day in 1970 and then declined over the following decade.

events.title: Publication of Silent Spring
events.description: Rachel Carson's book *Silent Spring* was published, establishing scientific evidence as a central pillar of environmental arguments and shaping the move toward evidence‑based environmental policies. Rachel Carson's book Silent Spring linked the dangers of the atomic bomb to the misuse of pesticides, emphasizing humanity's capacity to destroy nature and itself. Rachel Carson’s bestselling book Silent Spring brought the dangers of DDT aerial spraying to widespread public attention.
events.supporting_text: Rachel Carson's book Silent Spring (1962) was among the first to link the dangers of the atomic bomb to the misuse of pesticides, emphasising humanity's capacity to destroy nature and itself.
supporting_texts: Rachel Carson's book Silent Spring (1962) was among the first to link the dangers of the atomic bomb to the misuse of pesticides, emphasising humanity's capacity to destroy nature and itself.
In 1962, Rachel Carson brought DDT aerial spraying to widespread public attention through her bestselling book Silent Spring
Since the publication of Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962), the use of scientific evidence has become one of the central ways in which environmental arguments have been constructed.

significance.justification: Marked a turning point that made scientific evidence central to environmental arguments and policy.

events.title: Development of environmentalism as part of popular culture
events.description: A multi‑decadal process in which environmentalism became integrated into mainstream Western popular culture, characterized by countercultural roots, the rise of consumerism, media influence, and celebrity involvement over roughly the past sixty years.
events.supporting_text: This chapter has examined how environmentalism developed as part of popular culture over the past sixty years. In the 1960s, environmental issues burst into the public consciousness with unprecedented speed and urgency. During these early years, environmentalism had a clear countercultural element, and this has stayed with it over half a century of campaigns, protests and boycotts. The rise of consumerism, influence of the media and emergence of celebrity have all contributed to making environmentalism part of western mainstream culture.

significance.justification: Shows how environmentalism has become embedded in culture, indicating a systemic shift toward broader societal engagement with nature.
significance.supporting_text: This chapter has examined how environmentalism developed as part of popular culture over the past sixty years.

events.title: 2009 UK survey on green lifestyle perceptions

events.supporting_text: This confusion about what a green lifestyle actually entails is evident in the responses to a 2009 UK survey on the issue. A green lifestyle was no longer seen as an alternative lifestyle by half of the respondents, while a quarter of them disagreed that their lifestyle contributed to climate change. The majority of respondents (61 per cent) felt it was worth doing environmentally friendly things, while 55 per cent felt guilty when they do things that harm the planet.

significance.justification: The survey reveals public confusion and misperceptions about green lifestyles, diagnosing a barrier to harmony with nature.
significance.supporting_text: evident in the responses to a 2009 UK survey on the issue

events.title: Ongoing effort of the environmental movement to translate awareness into action and address consumerist values

concepts.supporting_text: 'A Blueprint for Survival' (The Ecologist, 1972) and Small is Beautiful (E. F. Schumacher, 1973) sketched out green alternatives.

concepts.name: environmental institutions
concepts.definition: Agencies, scientific programmes, international agreements, laws and regulations established to support environmental goals and give permanence to environmentalism.
concepts.supporting_text: Governments have responded to public concerns about the environment by establishing environmental institutions of their own. Agencies, scientific programmes, international agreements, laws and regulations have been set up to support environmental goals.

concepts.name: Environmental agenda
concepts.definition: The set of policy priorities and public discourse driven by scientific findings on environmental problems and their societal implications.
concepts.supporting_text: Over the past fifty years, science has driven the environmental agenda, explaining the cause and impact of environmental problems and the implications they have for society as a whole.
supporting_texts: Over the past fifty years, science has driven the environmental agenda, explaining the cause and impact of environmental problems and the implications they have for society as a whole.
The new social movement furthered the environmental agenda by mobilising public opinion and forcing governments and businesses to take action.
By 1988, environmental issues were at the top of the political agenda and dominated the election campaign.

significance.justification: Science is said to have driven the environmental agenda, shaping policy and public opinion, thus affecting salience.
significance.supporting_text: science has driven the environmental agenda, explaining the cause and impact of environmental problems and the implications they have for society as a whole.

concepts.name: counterculture
concepts.definition: A widespread tendency in the 1960s to question established values and institutions, emerging alongside opposition to the nuclear bomb, the Vietnam War, and chemical herbicides.
concepts.supporting_text: In the USA, growing opposition to the nuclear bomb, the Vietnam War and the use of chemical herbicide defoliants known as Agent Orange coincided with the emergence of a counterculture and an increasingly widespread tendency to question established values and institutions.

significance.justification: The counterculture signaled a shift in values that opened space for new environmental ideas.
significance.supporting_text: the emergence of a counterculture and an increasingly widespread tendency to question established values and institutions

concepts.name: New Left
concepts.definition: A political movement in France during the 1960s that attempted to overthrow the government, representing broader opposition to the state and industrial society.
concepts.supporting_text: In France, the New Left attempted to overthrow the government, while the American Students for a Democratic Society recruited members across university campuses.

significance.justification: The New Left’s challenge to existing political structures illustrated the possibility of systemic transformation.
significance.supporting_text: In France, the New Left attempted to overthrow the government

concepts.name: social movement
concepts.definition: A new and distinctive collective mobilization that emerged as a wave of campaigns and groups addressed emerging environmental issues.
concepts.supporting_text: As new environmental issues came to the fore, a wave of campaigns and groups emerged to tackle them, creating a new and distinctive social movement.

significance.justification: Described as a new and distinctive social movement, it organized collective action for environmental issues.
significance.supporting_text: a wave of campaigns and groups emerged to tackle them, creating a new and distinctive social movement

concepts.name: protected designation
concepts.definition: An approach, pioneered by the National Trust, to achieve formal protection status for specific natural areas.
concepts.supporting_text: Many early environmental groups followed the National Trust's approach to achieving protected designation for specific areas.

significance.justification: Seeking protected designation shows how legal mechanisms can re‑configure land‑use systems toward conservation.
significance.supporting_text: Many early environmental groups followed the National Trust’s approach to achieving protected designation for specific areas

concepts.name: throwaway society
concepts.definition: A societal model characterised by wastefulness, exemplified by the widespread use of non‑returnable bottles and a culture of disposability.
key_proponents: Friends of the Earth UK (FoE UK)
concepts.supporting_text: FoE UK launched its first campaign against non‑returnable bottles, linked to a wider message about the wastefulness of a throwaway society.
supporting_texts: FoE UK launched its first campaign against non‑returnable bottles, linked to a wider message about the wastefulness of a throwaway society.
The polystyrene 'clamshells' in which hamburgers were sold became a symbol of the throwaway society.

significance.justification: The term identifies the waste‑driven consumption pattern that the campaigns aimed to change.
significance.supporting_text: polystyrene ‘clamshells’ … became a symbol of the throwaway society.

concepts.name: green politics
concepts.definition: A political orientation that explicitly links social and environmental agendas, leading to the formation of new political parties across Europe.
concepts.supporting_text: Green politics was becoming more explicit as campaigners linked social and environmental agendas to create new political parties across Europe.

significance.justification: Emergence of green parties signals a shift toward integrating environmental goals into mainstream politics.
significance.supporting_text: Green politics was becoming more explicit as campaigners linked social and environmental agendas to create new political parties across Europe.

concepts.name: environmental lawsuits
concepts.definition: Legal actions initiated by scientists, legal experts and environmental NGOs to delay, halt, or force reconsideration of government and industrial activities that threaten the environment.
concepts.supporting_text: Scientists and legal experts either founded, or were employed by, new groups, and filed environmental lawsuits that delayed or halted government and industrial activities.

significance.justification: Legal actions are presented as a core strategy for the movement’s advocacy.
significance.supporting_text: law suits and legislative battles were to become a key feature of the US environmental movement.

concepts.name: grassroots democracy
concepts.definition: A form of democratic participation emphasizing local, bottom‑up decision‑making, identified as a core commitment of most European green parties.
concepts.supporting_text: most were committed to grassroots democracy, non-violence and social justice.

significance.justification: Promotes participatory decision‑making essential for collective environmental action.
significance.supporting_text: most were committed to grassroots democracy, non-violence and social justice

concepts.name: non-violence
concepts.definition: The principle of rejecting the use of force, cited as a central value of European green parties.
concepts.supporting_text: most were committed to grassroots democracy, non-violence and social justice.

significance.justification: Non‑violent principles underpin peaceful mobilisation for nature‑friendly policies.
significance.supporting_text: most were committed to grassroots democracy, non-violence and social justice

concepts.name: social justice
concepts.definition: A commitment to equitable distribution of resources and rights, listed among the core values of green parties in Europe.
concepts.supporting_text: most were committed to grassroots democracy, non-violence and social justice.

significance.justification: The commitment to social justice builds shared values that motivate collective environmental action.
significance.supporting_text: most were committed to grassroots democracy, non‑violence and social justice.

concepts.name: reduced‑hour working week
concepts.definition: A policy proposal calling for shorter standard work hours, promoted by the German Greens as part of their challenge to traditional economic growth models.
concepts.supporting_text: the German Greens used their platform to challenge traditional models of economic growth, called for a reduced-hour working week, and demanded an end to nuclear power.

significance.justification: Proposing a shorter work week signals a systemic shift in economic and social organization.
significance.supporting_text: German Greens ... called for a reduced‑hour working week

concepts.name: anti‑nuclear movement
concepts.definition: A social movement opposing nuclear energy and weapons, described as closely linked to the environmental movement in 1980s West Germany.
concepts.supporting_text: In 1980s West Germany, the anti-nuclear movement was almost identical to the environmental movement, and the Green Party acted as its parliamentary arm.

significance.justification: The movement mobilises citizens and parties around a concrete environmental goal.
significance.supporting_text: In 1980s West Germany, the anti‑nuclear movement was almost identical to the environmental movement

concepts.name: environmental activism
concepts.definition: Activism directed at ecological issues, which in the late Soviet period served as a relatively safe channel for criticizing the regime.
concepts.supporting_text: During the Soviet leadership of Mikhail Gorbachev (b. 1931) (1988-91), environmental activism in communist countries was seen as a safe way of criticising the Soviet regime, and environmental groups mobilised a great deal of public support.

significance.justification: Activism channels public support into political pressure for nature‑friendly policies.
significance.supporting_text: environmental activism in communist countries ... mobilised a great deal of public support

concepts.name: green parties
concepts.definition: Political parties whose primary focus is environmental protection and sustainability, emerging across Europe in the 1970s‑1990s as alternatives to traditional parties.
concepts.supporting_text: Green political parties established themselves throughout Europe and most western economies because existing parties were not able to address the environmental agenda adequately.

significance.justification: Green parties provide institutional channels for environmental demands.
significance.supporting_text: Green political parties established themselves throughout Europe

concepts.name: neither left nor right political positioning
concepts.definition: A self‑described stance of the early German Green movement, emphasizing a position beyond traditional left‑right divisions.
concepts.supporting_text: the fledgling German political movement set the tone with the slogan 'we are neither left or right: we are in front'.

significance.justification: Distinct positioning differentiates green politics, enhancing public recognition.
significance.supporting_text: we are neither left or right: we are in front

concepts.name: Green Party (UK)
concepts.definition: A political party focused on environmental issues that mobilised public discontent over nuclear power, the ozone layer, and the Poll Tax, winning 2.2 million votes (15 % of the vote) in the 1989 European Parliamentary Elections.
concepts.supporting_text: Sara Parkin (b. 1946), co‑secretary and spokesperson for the UK Green Party, was able to mobilise this discontent. In the 1989 European Parliamentary Elections, the UK Green Party won the support of 2.2 million people - equivalent to 15 per cent of the vote… it took until 2010 for Caroline Lucas (b. 1960) to be elected as Britain's first Green Party Member of Parliament.

concepts.name: Transboundary pollution
concepts.definition: The recognition that pollution crosses national borders, forming part of the emerging understanding that drove high‑profile global environmental campaigns in the 1970s.
concepts.supporting_text: By the 1970s, a new breed of environmental organisation had emerged that led high‑profile environmental campaigns aimed at a global impact. This reflected an understanding of transboundary pollution, and a growing recognition of habitat destruction and the threat it posed to wildlife.

concepts.name: Habitat destruction
concepts.definition: The process of degrading or eliminating natural habitats, identified in the 1970s as a major threat to wildlife and a driver of global environmental campaigns.
concepts.supporting_text: This reflected an understanding of transboundary pollution, and a growing recognition of habitat destruction and the threat it posed to wildlife.

significance.justification: The text highlights habitat destruction as a major threat to wildlife, exposing a damaging environmental condition.
significance.supporting_text: a growing recognition of habitat destruction and the threat it posed to wildlife

concepts.name: Fundraising strategies (environmental NGOs)
concepts.definition: New approaches developed by WWF to raise large sums of money for environmental action, exemplified by a 1961 British fundraising appeal that raised US$1.9 million in its first three years.
concepts.supporting_text: What made WWF a thoroughly modern campaign group was its focus on the need to raise funds for environmental action, and as a consequence it developed new fundraising strategies. In 1961, WWF launched its first British fundraising appeal… In its first three years, US$1.9 million was donated to projects across Africa, Europe and India.

significance.justification: New fundraising strategies enabled WWF to raise large sums for projects, building capacity for environmental action.
significance.supporting_text: What made WWF a thoroughly modern campaign group was its focus on the need to raise funds for environmental action, and as a consequence it developed new fundraising strategies.

concepts.name: Quaker philosophy of bearing witness
concepts.definition: A philosophical approach that emphasizes passive resistance and the presence of campaigners at sites of environmental problems, forming a foundational ethic for Greenpeace campaigns.
concepts.supporting_text: The Quaker philosophy of bearing witness, demonstrating passive resistance by placing campaigners at the scene of environmental problems has been fundamental to Greenpeace campaigns ever since.

significance.justification: The philosophy underpins Greenpeace’s passive‑resistance tactics, enabling coordinated activism.
significance.supporting_text: The Quaker philosophy of bearing witness, demonstrating passive resistance ... has been fundamental to Greenpeace campaigns ever since.

concepts.name: First‑past‑the‑post electoral system
concepts.definition: The British electoral system in which the candidate with the most votes in each constituency wins, cited as a factor limiting the Green Party’s ability to win seats.
concepts.supporting_text: This has been attributed to a number of causes, including the British first‑past‑the‑post electoral system, and resistance within the Green Party to reforms intended to make it more electable.

significance.justification: The system is cited as a cause for the Green Party’s failure to win seats, exposing a structural barrier.
significance.supporting_text: including the British first-past-the post electoral system

concepts.name: Environmental justice movement
concepts.definition: A US‑based grassroots movement that emerged in the 1980s, framed by racial discrimination and concerns over environmental pollution, and distinguished from established environmental groups by its focus on the intersection of social, economic and environmental justice.
concepts.supporting_text: The US environmental justice ... emerged in response to planning decisions that appeared to give priority to private or government interests over community interests. The environmental justice movement emerged against a backdrop of wider public concern over environmental pollution in the USA, but was framed by the issue of racial discrimination.

significance.justification: The concept reframed environmental issues through a lens of racial and social equity, shifting public discourse.
significance.supporting_text: environmental justice movement

concepts.name: Anti‑roads movement
concepts.definition: A single‑issue campaign in the UK that opposes large‑scale road‑building programmes, emerging in the early 1990s and supported by a broad coalition of environmental and community groups.
concepts.supporting_text: The UK anti‑roads movement is an example of a single‑issue campaign that was supported by a wide range of groups from inside and outside the environmental movement. It emerged in the early 1990s with renewed public interest in the environment.
supporting_texts: The UK anti‑roads movement is an example of a single‑issue campaign that was supported by a wide range of groups from inside and outside the environmental movement. It emerged in the early 1990s with renewed public interest in the environment.

The UK anti‑roads movements emerged in response to planning decisions that appeared to give priority to private or government interests over community interests. The UK anti‑roads movement had strong countercultural roots and drew on a long tradition of direct action in the country.

significance.justification: Described as a single‑issue campaign that united diverse groups to oppose road building.
significance.supporting_text: The UK anti‑roads movement is an example of a single‑issue campaign that was supported by a wide range of groups.

concepts.name: Direct action
concepts.definition: A tactic of physically intervening to disrupt activities deemed harmful, exemplified by high‑speed inflatable boats blocking whaling ships and other confrontational methods used by environmental activists.
concepts.supporting_text: Many participants were influenced by tactics used by Greenpeace, Earth First! and the peace movement, including the women's peace camps at the Royal Air Force Base at Greenham Common.

significance.justification: Direct action provides a tactical toolkit for activists to exert pressure and achieve concrete outcomes.
significance.supporting_text: long tradition of direct action in the country

concepts.name: Global countercultural movement
concepts.definition: A 1990s worldwide movement that combined environmental, social and economic justice concerns, linking established and grassroots groups across the environmental spectrum.
concepts.supporting_text: This led to new and distinctive coalitions and campaign tactics that contributed to the development of the 1990s global countercultural movement.

significance.justification: The movement linked diverse groups, creating a platform for systemic cultural transformation.
significance.supporting_text: development of the 1990s global countercultural movement

concepts.name: Environmental racism
concepts.definition: The pattern whereby race is the strongest predictor of where hazardous waste facilities are sited, prompting a national movement to oppose such inequitable siting.
key_proponents: United Church of Christ's Commission for Racial Justice
concepts.supporting_text: In 1987, the United Church of Christ's Commission for Racial Justice published Toxic Wastes and Race. The study found that race was the strongest variable in predicting the siting of waste facilities. This galvanised the movement nationally to oppose environmental racism.

significance.justification: Identified as the strongest predictor of waste‑facility siting, revealing a systemic injustice.
significance.supporting_text: The study found that race was the strongest variable in predicting the siting of waste facilities.

concepts.name: Civil disobedience (in road protests)
concepts.definition: A tactic where activists shift from courtroom battles to direct, on‑the‑ground obstruction of road‑building projects, exemplified by protest camps such as Twyford Down.
concepts.supporting_text: As new road schemes reached the implementation stage, this civil disobedience moved from courtrooms to the planned road routes. Twyford Down was the first road protest camp to hit the national news in 1991.

significance.justification: Direct actions such as occupying sites and locking to trees were used to disrupt road projects.
significance.supporting_text: By occupying and locking themselves to trees, digging tunnels and doing everything they could to disrupt road‑building operations...

concepts.name: Direct action (non‑violent)
concepts.definition: A form of protest involving occupation of sites, tree‑locking, tunnel digging and other disruptive tactics to impede road‑building, creating a new public image of modern environmentalists.
concepts.supporting_text: Newly established non‑violent direct action groups such as Earth First! (a US import) and Reclaim the Streets organised, or were present at, many road protest camps. By occupying and locking themselves to trees, digging tunnels and doing everything they could to disrupt road‑building operations, they developed a new public image of the modern environmentalist.

significance.justification: Non‑violent direct action is presented as a tactic that enabled limited‑resource groups to affect road‑building costs.
significance.supporting_text: they developed a new public image of the modern environmentalist... could use direct action to damage the reputation and increase the financial costs...

concepts.name: anti‑globalisation movement
concepts.definition: A loosely coordinated protest movement of the late 1990s that brought together a broad range of participants and linked social, economic and environmental issues in opposition to globalisation.
concepts.supporting_text: The anti‑globalisation protests of the late 1990s had distinctive organisational features. They were loosely coordinated, involved a broad range of participants, and linked together a wide range of social, economic and environmental issues.

significance.justification: The movement linked diverse campaigns, showing systemic interconnections.
significance.supporting_text: A global network of individuals and organisations grew out of this series of coordinated protests.

concepts.name: World Social Forum
concepts.definition: A recurring global gathering that provides a venue for civil‑society networks, including environmental groups, to meet and develop collaborative actions; it has met on a regular basis since 2001.
concepts.supporting_text: These networks continue to develop through a number of avenues such as the World Social Forum, which has met on a regular basis since 2001.

significance.justification: The concept provides a recurring venue for coordinated civil‑society action.
significance.supporting_text: These networks continue to develop through a number of avenues such as the World Social Forum, which has met on a regular basis since 2001.

concepts.name: independent media centre
concepts.definition: A grassroots online platform created by activists to allow anyone to upload news and reports from protest events, exemplified by the site set up after the 1989 WTO Seattle protests.
concepts.supporting_text: When activists established an independent media centre for anyone to upload news and reports from the 1989 WTO Seattle protests, the website received over a million hits over a couple of days.

significance.justification: Provided an online platform that enabled rapid sharing of protest information, amplifying coordination.
significance.supporting_text: When activists established an independent media centre for anyone to upload news and reports from the 1989 WTO Seattle protests, the website received over a million hits over a couple of days.

concepts.name: global network of civil society organisations
concepts.definition: A loosely connected worldwide network of individuals and organisations that emerged from coordinated anti‑globalisation protests and continues to develop through shared platforms and events.
concepts.supporting_text: A global network of individuals and organisations grew out of this series of coordinated protests.

significance.justification: Emerged from coordinated protests, linking diverse groups worldwide for joint environmental action.
significance.supporting_text: A global network of individuals and organisations grew out of this series of coordinated protests.

concepts.name: anti‑consumerism
concepts.definition: A worldview and set of practices that reject consumerist culture and corporate dominance, exemplified by campaigns such as Buy Nothing Day.
concepts.supporting_text: The anti‑consumerist Buy Nothing Day, first launched in the USA in 1992, encapsulated the ideals of this countercultural movement.

significance.justification: Frames consumerism as a systemic driver of environmental harm, highlighting a prevailing unsustainable condition.
significance.supporting_text: The anti‑consumerist Buy Nothing Day, first launched in the USA in 1992, encapsulated the ideals of this countercultural movement.

concepts.name: Internet activism
concepts.definition: Activism that can be undertaken from the comfort of home, described as cheap, easy and effective, and used to mobilise supporters worldwide for environmental campaigns.
concepts.supporting_text: Internet activism can be undertaken from the comfort of home, and is cheap, easy and effective. In 2006, Greenpeace launched the Green My Apple campaign... it now mobilises internet activists across the globe to support its campaigns.

significance.justification: Identified as cheap, easy, and effective means for mass participation.
significance.supporting_text: Internet activism can be undertaken from the comfort of home, and is cheap, easy and effective.

concepts.name: Partnership model
concepts.definition: An approach where environmental groups shift focus from recruiting individual members to establishing collaborations with governments and corporations to embed conservation or sustainability into business practices.
concepts.supporting_text: Over the past thirty years, some environmental groups have shifted their focus from recruiting members of the public to establishing partnerships with governments and corporations. The US‑based group Conservation International (est. 1987) partnered with other organisations... Groups tackling a wide range of environmental issues now take this approach...

significance.justification: Highlights a governance approach that can re‑configure sector dynamics.
significance.supporting_text: Shift of environmental groups toward partnership models (multi‑year process) ... based on Partnership model.

concepts.name: Membership‑based model
concepts.definition: A strategy that relies on a large base of individual members and supporters to fund campaigns and maintain organisational independence.
key_proponents: Royal Society for the Protection of Birds
concepts.supporting_text: These differences can be seen in the way groups have directed and funded their campaigns: for some, a large membership base is as important as it was in the 1960s... FoE International claims over 2 million members and supporters, and the NRDC illustrates its strength by referring to its 1.3 million members and online activists.

significance.justification: Membership builds a constituency and resources for environmental action.
significance.supporting_text: FoE International claims over 2 million members and supporters... NRDC illustrates its strength by referring to its 1.3 million members.

concepts.name: Crowded marketplace
concepts.definition: A metaphor describing the competitive environment in which new environmental campaigns must vie for attention, funding, and impact alongside many other initiatives.
concepts.supporting_text: Every new environmental campaign enters a crowded market place, where messaging, branding and impact are sometimes as important as the environmental goal.

significance.justification: Describes competition for attention and funding among groups.
significance.supporting_text: Every new environmental campaign enters a crowded market place, where messaging, branding and impact are sometimes as important as the environmental goal.

concepts.name: Wise Use Movement
concepts.definition: A counter‑movement that opposes environmental causes, often industry‑led and receiving popular support.
concepts.supporting_text: The counter‑movement has taken many forms, including the Wise Use Movement and the Global Climate Coalition (see Chapters 4 and 7); often these are industry‑led and have received popular support.

significance.justification: Described as an industry‑led counter‑movement that opposes environmental causes.
significance.supporting_text: Counter‑movements ... include the Wise Use Movement ... often these are industry‑led and have received popular support.

concepts.name: Global Climate Coalition
concepts.definition: An organised industry‑led opposition to environmental causes that has garnered popular support.
concepts.supporting_text: The counter‑movement has taken many forms, including the Wise Use Movement and the Global Climate Coalition (see Chapters 4 and 7); often these are industry‑led and have received popular support.

significance.justification: Identified as an organised opposition that challenges environmental initiatives.
significance.supporting_text: Counter‑movements ... include the ... Global Climate Coalition (see Chapters 4 and 7); often these are industry‑led.

concepts.name: Low‑carbon economy
concepts.definition: An economic transition aimed at reducing carbon emissions, as targeted by the UK Climate Change Act.
concepts.supporting_text: The Act aims to enable the UK to make the transition to a low‑carbon economy, and resulted in the independent Committee on Climate Change being established to provide advice to government on these targets and related policies.

significance.justification: The concept signals a systemic shift toward sustainable production and consumption.
significance.supporting_text: The Act aims to enable the UK to make the transition to a low-carbon economy.

concepts.name: Legally binding targets
concepts.definition: World’s first legally binding targets to reduce six greenhouse gases by 80 % by 2050 compared with a 1990 baseline, set by the 2008 Climate Change Act.
concepts.supporting_text: the UK government to adopt the 2008 Climate Change Act, which set the world’s first legally binding targets to reduce six greenhouse gases by 80 per cent by 2050 compared with a 1990 baseline.
supporting_texts: the UK government to adopt the 2008 Climate Change Act, which set the world’s first legally binding targets to reduce six greenhouse gases by 80 per cent by 2050 compared with a 1990 baseline.
a move that was essential in order for other major economies to do a deal.

significance.justification: Binding targets are essential for achieving measurable emissions reductions.
significance.supporting_text: raised the possibility of US agreement to legally binding targets

concepts.name: The Big Ask campaign
concepts.definition: A campaign launched by Friends of the Earth (FoE) and public figures to create momentum for strong, binding climate legislation, first in the UK and later across Europe.
concepts.supporting_text: In particular, the FoE's The Big Ask campaign helped create the public momentum needed for the UK government to adopt the 2008 Climate Change Act… Thom Yorke (b. 1968), lead singer of the music group Radiohead, launched The Big Ask campaign on 25 May 2005.

significance.justification: The campaign mobilised citizens and MPs, directly influencing climate legislation.
significance.supporting_text: FoE’s The Big Ask campaign helped create the public momentum needed for the UK government to adopt the 2008 Climate Change Act.

concepts.name: Carbon scam
concepts.definition: A term used by Greenpeace to describe the Noel Kempff Climate Action Project, alleging that it did not deliver scientifically quantifiable carbon emissions reductions or sustainable benefits.
concepts.supporting_text: It described the project as a 'carbon scam', contradicted claims that it produced scientifically quantifiable carbon emissions reductions, and called into question whether it had provided sustainable benefits and alternative livelihoods to local communities.

significance.justification: Labeling the project a ‘carbon scam’ highlights misleading carbon‑offset practices.
significance.supporting_text: Greenpeace ... described the project as a ‘carbon scam’.

concepts.name: Counter‑movement
concepts.definition: The organised opposition to environmental causes that emerges alongside the environmental movement, often industry‑led and sometimes receiving popular support.
concepts.supporting_text: In several countries, and in the USA in particular, countermovements have been established to oppose environmental causes. The counter‑movement has taken many forms, including the Wise Use Movement and the Global Climate Coalition…

significance.justification: Counter‑movements are organized to oppose environmental initiatives.
significance.supporting_text: countermovements have been established to oppose environmental causes.

concepts.name: cap-and-trade system
concepts.definition: A market‑based mechanism that sets a cap on overall emissions and then requires companies in the energy and transport sectors to obtain emission allowances to emit greenhouse gases.
concepts.supporting_text: The Bill is based on a 'cap-and-trade' system - a market-based mechanism that sets a cap on overall emissions and then requires companies in the energy and transport sectors to obtain emission allowances to emit greenhouse gases.

significance.justification: Market‑based mechanism offers a pathway to lower national emissions.
significance.supporting_text: The Bill is based on a ‘cap‑and‑trade’ system – a market‑based mechanism that sets a cap on overall emissions...

concepts.name: Transition Towns movement
concepts.definition: A community‑led response to climate change and peak oil, with over 250 transition towns and cities in twelve countries working to raise awareness of green living.
concepts.supporting_text: In the UK, the Transition Towns movement has provided a community‑led response to climate change and peak oil. There are over 250 transition towns and cities, spanning twelve countries, working to raise awareness of green living.

significance.justification: Community‑led initiative mobilises local actors toward sustainable practices.
significance.supporting_text: In the UK, the Transition Towns movement has provided a community‑led response to climate change and peak oil.

concepts.name: Interfaith Power and Light network
concepts.definition: A religious‑based network in the United States that provides a faith‑focused response to climate change.
concepts.supporting_text: In the USA, the Interfaith Power and Light network has provided a religious response to climate change.

significance.justification: Religious groups coordinate climate action, expanding the movement’s moral base.
significance.supporting_text: In the USA, the Interfaith Power and Light network has provided a religious response to climate change.

concepts.name: MoveOn network
concepts.definition: A progressive online network with approximately 3 million members in the United States that has consistently made energy and environmental issues a campaign priority since 2003.
concepts.supporting_text: The progressive MoveOn network has approximately 3 million members across the USA, and since 2003 has consistently made energy and environmental issues a campaign priority.

significance.justification: Large membership and sustained campaigning amplify environmental advocacy.
significance.supporting_text: The progressive MoveOn network has approximately 3 million members across the USA, and since 2003 has consistently made energy and environmental issues a campaign priority.

concepts.name: Avaaz
concepts.definition: A web‑based campaign community that uses the model pioneered by MoveOn and claims 3.3 million members across 192 countries, campaigning on a wide range of social, economic and environmental issues, including climate change.
concepts.supporting_text: Avaaz, a web‑based campaign community, uses the model pioneered by MoveOn. It claims 3.3 million members across 192 countries, and campaigns on a wide range of social, economic and environmental issues, including climate change.

significance.justification: Web‑based platform enables rapid, global mobilisation for climate causes.
significance.supporting_text: Avaaz, a web‑based campaign community, uses the model pioneered by MoveOn. It claims 3.3 million members across 192 countries...

concepts.name: 350 campaign
concepts.definition: An international climate‑change campaign that focused on achieving 350 parts per million of carbon dioxide, organising a global day of action with 5,200 demonstrations in 181 countries.
concepts.supporting_text: In 2009, the campaign group 350 organised the single largest international campaign on climate change. The campaign focused on achieving 350 parts per million of carbon dioxide... Through the internet and other media channels, the 350 campaign organised a global day of action. A total of 5200 demonstrations took place in 181 countries.

significance.justification: Mobilised the largest international climate campaign and a global day of action.
significance.supporting_text: In 2009, the campaign group 350 organised the single largest international campaign on climate change... organised a global day of action. A total of 5200 demonstrations took place in 181 countries

concepts.name: Anti‑consumerism counter‑culture
concepts.definition: A cultural strand within environmentalism that opposes excessive consumption and promotes alternative values and lifestyles aligned with ecological sustainability.
concepts.supporting_text: …from its early beginnings in nature conservation to the rise of a global anti‑consumerism counter‑culture.

significance.justification: Signals a cultural shift away from consumption that could transform system dynamics.
significance.supporting_text: rise of a global anti-consumerism counter‑culture.

concepts.name: Issue‑attention cycle
concepts.definition: A pattern whereby environmental problems gain public and media prominence after scientific discovery, prompting campaign action, but then lose attention over time as the issue becomes costly and difficult to address, often fading from public consciousness.

concepts.supporting_text: This argument was shared by Ernst F. Schumacher (1911‑77), who championed the use of appropriate technology in Small is Beautiful: A Study of Economics as if People Mattered (1973).

significance.justification: Promotes technology suited to ecological limits, challenging high‑intensity industrial approaches.
significance.supporting_text: This argument was shared by Ernst F. Schumacher … who championed the use of appropriate technology.

concepts.name: Ecological economics
concepts.definition: A field of study that integrates ecological constraints and economic analysis, founded on the works of Boulding, Georgescu‑Roegen, and Schumacher.
concepts.supporting_text: Combined together, the works of Boulding, Georgescu‑Roegen and Schumacher provided the foundation for modern‑day ecological economics.
supporting_texts: Combined together, the works of Boulding, Georgescu‑Roegen and Schumacher provided the foundation for modern‑day ecological economics.
Ecological economics is as much about ensuring the environment is recognised in standard economic theory as setting out an alternative to a capitalist (or communist) economic system.
This chapter has examined how ecological economics has developed as a discipline that is critical of standard economic theories while at the same time making use of them.

Ultimately, ecological economics aims to address the interdependence of economies and ecosystems, particularly how these two systems can co‑evolve based on principles of sustainable development - equity, intergenerational justice and personal responsibility, and improvement of human wellbeing.

significance.justification: Offers a theoretical basis for aligning economies with ecosystem limits.
significance.supporting_text: Ultimately, ecological economics aims to address the interdependence of economies and ecosystems...

concepts.name: Steady‑state economy (SSE)
concepts.definition: An economic model characterized by constant population and constant stock of capital, maintained by a low rate of material and energy throughput that stays within the regenerative and assimilative capacities of the ecosystem.
concepts.supporting_text: Daly is most strongly associated with his attempt to articulate an alternative approach to the conventional growth paradigm in the form of the steady‑state economy (SSE). ... following [John Stuart] Mill we might define a SSE as an economy with constant population and constant stock of capital, maintained by a low rate of throughput that is within the regenerative and assimilative capacities of the ecosystem.

significance.justification: Proposes an economy with constant population and capital, operating within ecosystem capacities.
significance.supporting_text: Daly is most strongly associated with … the steady‑state economy (SSE).

concepts.name: Sustainable economic welfare index
concepts.definition: An index designed to replace GNP as a measure of economic wellbeing, reflecting sustainable welfare rather than purely monetary output.
concepts.supporting_text: Daly and John B. Cobb (b. 1925) constructed an index of sustainable economic welfare intended to replace GNP as a measure of economic wellbeing.

significance.justification: Offers a concrete tool for policymakers to assess wellbeing beyond GDP.
significance.supporting_text: Daly and John B. Cobb constructed an index of sustainable economic welfare intended to replace GNP as a measure of economic wellbeing.

concepts.name: Ecological footprint
concepts.definition: A metric that quantifies the amount of biologically productive land and water area required to supply the resources a population consumes and to assimilate its wastes.
concepts.supporting_text: Measures such as the ecological footprint, genuine progress indicator and happy planet index have been applied to national economies...

significance.justification: Illustrates that alternative metrics have yet to supplant GDP, highlighting the dominance of conventional measures.
significance.supporting_text: Measures such as the ecological footprint … have been applied … but none has supplanted economic measures as the primary measure of a country’s progress.

concepts.name: Genuine progress indicator
concepts.definition: A composite metric that attempts to measure economic progress by accounting for environmental and social factors, not just monetary output.
concepts.supporting_text: Measures such as the ecological footprint, genuine progress indicator and happy planet index have been applied to national economies...

significance.justification: Shows limited uptake of alternative wellbeing indicators compared with GDP.
significance.supporting_text: Measures such as the ecological footprint, genuine progress indicator … have been applied … but none has supplanted economic measures as the primary measure of a country’s progress.

concepts.name: Happy planet index
concepts.definition: An indicator that combines well‑being, life expectancy and ecological footprint to assess how efficiently nations deliver long and happy lives for their citizens while using few natural resources.
concepts.supporting_text: Measures such as the ecological footprint, genuine progress indicator and happy planet index have been applied to national economies...

significance.justification: Shows an alternative metric that could shift how progress is measured toward wellbeing.
significance.supporting_text: Measures such as the ecological footprint, genuine progress indicator and happy planet index have been applied to national economies...

concepts.name: Cost‑benefit analysis
concepts.definition: A methodological tool widely used to make the case for environmental protection and to choose between different environmental protection options, though its application can be complex, controversial, and not always trusted by environmental campaigners or regulated industries.
concepts.supporting_text: Cost‑benefit analysis has been widely used to make the case for environmental protection and to choose between different environmental protection options. Agencies responsible for environmental regulations such as the EPA in the USA have used cost‑benefit analysis extensively.

significance.justification: Widely used yet controversial tool that can mask multiple environmental values.
significance.supporting_text: Cost–benefit analysis has been widely used… but its application can be complex and controversial and is not always trusted.

concepts.name: Social cost‑benefit analysis
concepts.definition: An extension of cost‑benefit analysis that incorporates social costs, used in the Roskill Commission’s proposal for a third runway in London to evaluate impacts such as noise pollution.
concepts.supporting_text: When the Roskill Commission proposed a location for a third runway in London in the early 1970s, it used social cost‑benefit analysis to support its case.

significance.justification: Attempts to incorporate social and environmental dimensions into economic appraisal.
significance.supporting_text: When the Roskill Commission… used social cost‑benefit analysis to support its case.

concepts.name: Ecosystem services
concepts.definition: A conceptual framework that relates the functioning of ecosystems to the provision of services (provisioning, regulating, cultural, and supporting) that contribute to human wellbeing, translating ecological functions into economic language that highlights their human utility and value.
concepts.supporting_text: An approach to communicating this in a structured way has its origins in the 1970s, when the functioning of ecosystems was related to the provision of services... Holdren and Ehrlich advocated this idea... The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment... defined the four categories of ecosystem services... Robert Costanza and colleagues attempted to estimate the value of ecosystem services provided by the Earth's biosphere.

significance.justification: Core framework translating ecological functions into human‑centred value terms.
significance.supporting_text: The power of the ecosystem services approach is that it provides a way for economists to translate ecological functions… into a language that makes clear their human utility and value.

concepts.name: Public service functions of the environment
concepts.definition: The idea that the environment provides services to the public, a concept articulated by Holdren and Ehrlich as part of the early ecosystem services discourse.
concepts.supporting_text: Holdren and Ehrlich advocated this idea and in an article for American Scientist described the 'public service functions of the environment'.

significance.justification: Frames environmental benefits as public services, broadening societal recognition.
significance.supporting_text: Holdren and Ehrlich… described the ‘public service functions of the environment’.

concepts.name: Market failures
concepts.definition: Economic situations where negative externalities, such as environmental 'bads', are not reflected in market prices, requiring correction through taxes or other policy instruments.
concepts.supporting_text: Because many ecosystem services are not recognised in the market system, the full cost of their degradation is not considered. Following Pigou, these negative externalities should be regarded as market failures and corrected.

significance.justification: Identifies why environmental costs are omitted from market signals.
significance.supporting_text: Following Pigou, these negative externalities should be regarded as market failures and corrected.

concepts.name: Market failure
concepts.definition: A situation where the market does not allocate resources efficiently; Stern described climate change as the greatest scale of market failure the world has seen.
concepts.supporting_text: Sir Nicholas Stern (b. 1946) described climate change as 'market failure on the greatest scale the world has seen'.

significance.justification: Stern labels climate change as a massive market failure, diagnosing a systemic economic problem.
significance.supporting_text: Sir Nicholas Stern ... described climate change as ‘market failure on the greatest scale the world has seen’.

concepts.name: Discount rate
concepts.definition: A factor used in economic analysis to convert future values into present values; low rates give more weight to the future, high rates give less weight.
concepts.supporting_text: At the heart of this debate is the valuation of the future; economic analysis typically applies discount rates to values in future years to make them directly comparable with present values. Low discount rates make the future more important, high discount rates make it less so. Stern used a near-zero discount rate to underpin his argument; ... Some economists, such as William Nordhaus (b. 1941), use much higher discount rates...

significance.justification: Different discount rates lead to divergent policy conclusions, showing their pivotal role in system outcomes.
significance.supporting_text: Low discount rates make the future more important, high discount rates make it less so.

concepts.name: Insurance approach to climate policy
concepts.definition: Treating climate‑change policy as insurance against worst‑case scenarios rather than as a cost‑benefit analysis exercise.
concepts.supporting_text: As an alternative approach, some economists argue that climate change policy should be treated as insurance against worst-case scenarios rather than a measure that can be subjected to cost‑benefit analysis.

significance.justification: Framing climate policy as insurance suggests a non‑cost‑benefit pathway, opening new systemic possibilities.
significance.supporting_text: some economists argue that climate change policy should be treated as insurance against worst-case scenarios...

concepts.name: Carbon pricing
concepts.definition: The establishment of a monetary price on carbon emissions by governments to internalise the climate cost of emitting CO₂.
concepts.supporting_text: Although the debate regarding the economics of climate change continues, governments have acted to establish a price for carbon.

significance.justification: Carbon pricing mechanisms (ETS, Kyoto) mobilise economic incentives for emission reductions.
significance.supporting_text: governments have acted to establish a price for carbon. The EU has established an emissions trading scheme, and the Kyoto Protocol...

concepts.name: Pricing of ecosystem services
concepts.definition: Assigning monetary value to the benefits that ecosystems provide, enabling businesses to account for these services in economic decisions.
concepts.supporting_text: Business has much to gain from the pricing of ecosystem services, but it also has potentially enormous environmental liabilities.

significance.justification: Valuing ecosystem services creates market signals that can guide business behaviour toward sustainability.
significance.supporting_text: Business has much to gain from the pricing of ecosystem services...

concepts.name: No net loss
concepts.definition: A business initiative in which a company's environmental impacts are offset by undertaking environmental activities of at least equal value.
concepts.supporting_text: In recognition of these issues, some business sectors are exploring 'no net loss' ... initiatives in which their impacts are offset by undertaking environmental activities of at least equal value.

significance.justification: The ‘no net loss’ initiative encourages firms to offset impacts, fostering proactive environmental stewardship.
significance.supporting_text: some business sectors are exploring ‘no net loss’ or ‘net positive impact’ initiatives...

concepts.name: Net positive impact
concepts.definition: A business initiative aiming to create environmental benefits that exceed the company's own environmental impacts.
concepts.supporting_text: In recognition of these issues, some business sectors are exploring ... 'net positive impact' initiatives in which their impacts are offset by undertaking environmental activities of at least equal value.

concepts.name: Mutual coercion mutually agreed upon
concepts.definition: Hardin’s proposed solution to the tragedy of the commons, whereby collective, mutually accepted constraints are imposed to prevent over‑exploitation.
concepts.supporting_text: His solution was 'mutual coercion mutually agreed upon'.

concepts.name: Privatisation of natural resources
concepts.definition: The idea of treating commonly owned natural resources, such as water, as economic goods that can be owned, priced, and managed by private sector actors.
concepts.supporting_text: Hardin's ideas have been used to support the privatisation of commonly owned resources... The idea of privatisation of natural resources has proved particularly controversial in relation to water usage.

significance.justification: The text links privatisation to market‑based water pricing that can exclude low‑income groups.
significance.supporting_text: Hardin’s ideas have been used to support the privatisation of commonly owned resources… pricing of water resources… low‑income groups may find they are priced out.

concepts.name: Ecosystem services approach
concepts.definition: A framework that recognises the economic value of ecosystem functions and supports pricing of natural resources (e.g., water) to incentivise careful use.
concepts.supporting_text: This is in line with the ecosystem services approach and supports the pricing of water resources so as to incentivise careful use in the developed and developing worlds.

significance.justification: The approach justifies assigning economic value to water, suggesting a shift toward incentive‑based conservation.
significance.supporting_text: This is in line with the ecosystem services approach and supports the pricing of water resources so as to incentivise careful use.

concepts.name: Universal right to water and sanitation
concepts.definition: The principle that access to basic water and sanitation is a universal human right and should not be treated as a commodity that can be negotiated.
concepts.supporting_text: Civil society groups have argued that 'access to basic water and sanitation are universal rights, and cannot therefore be negotiated as commodities'.

significance.justification: Civil‑society groups invoke this right to oppose commodification, mobilising advocacy.
significance.supporting_text: Civil society groups have argued that ‘access to basic water and sanitation are universal rights, and cannot therefore be negotiated as commodities’.

concepts.name: Cooperative institutions for commons governance
concepts.definition: Durable, cooperative institutions that are organised and governed by the resource users themselves, designed to resolve the problem of the commons.
concepts.supporting_text: According to Ostrom, an approach to resolving the problem of the commons is the design of durable, cooperative institutions that are organised and governed by the resource users themselves.

significance.justification: Ostrom proposes user‑governed institutions as an alternative to top‑down control, indicating a systemic governance shift.
significance.supporting_text: According to Ostrom, an approach… is the design of durable, cooperative institutions that are organised and governed by the resource users themselves.

concepts.name: Global Green New Deal (GGND)
concepts.definition: An initiative launched by UNEP in December 2008 that proposes an economic stimulus package aimed at reviving the global economy while creating jobs, reducing carbon dependency, ending extreme poverty, and prioritising spending on energy efficiency, sustainable transport, renewable energy, agricultural productivity, freshwater management and sanitation.
concepts.supporting_text: Following in his footsteps, UNEP instigated the Global Green New Deal (GGND) initiative in December 2008. The GGND included an economic stimulus package aimed at reviving the global economy recovery, creating jobs, reducing carbon dependency and environmental degradation, and ending extreme world poverty by 2015.

significance.justification: The GGND outlines a coordinated global response that integrates economic recovery with environmental goals.
significance.supporting_text: The GGND included an economic stimulus package aimed at reviving the global economy… creating jobs, reducing carbon dependency and environmental degradation.

concepts.name: Green fiscal spending
concepts.definition: Policy recommendation that the world’s richest economies should allocate a share of GDP (e.g., 1 % of global GDP) to environmental initiatives and support green fiscal measures at global and national levels.
concepts.supporting_text: It recommended that the world's richest economies should spend 1 per cent of global GDP on environmental initiatives over the coming years, and make policy changes at global and national levels to support green fiscal spending.

significance.justification: The recommendation to allocate 1 % of global GDP to environmental initiatives calls for coordinated policy action.
significance.supporting_text: It recommended that the world’s richest economies should spend 1 per cent of global GDP on environmental initiatives over the coming years.

concepts.name: Green stimulus
concepts.definition: Fiscal spending by G20 governments that includes a sizeable green fiscal component aimed at low‑carbon investments, representing 16 % of all fiscal spending during the recession and 0.7 % of G20 GDP.
key_proponents: G20 governments (UK, USA, China, South Korea, EU)
concepts.supporting_text: During the recession, members of the G20 spent over US$520 billion on a green stimulus. The stimulus comprised 16 per cent of all fiscal spending and 0.7 per cent of the G20 GDP...

significance.justification: Represents a policy lever that can shift investment patterns toward sustainability.
significance.supporting_text: During the recession, members of the G20 spent over US$520 billion on a green stimulus.

concepts.name: Green fiscal component
concepts.definition: The portion of fiscal stimulus dedicated to green investments such as low‑carbon projects, renewable energy, mass transit, and smart‑grid infrastructure.
concepts.supporting_text: In 2009, some G20 governments adopted policies to boost aggregate demand and growth, which included a sizeable green fiscal component. The UK devoted approximately 11 per cent of its US$3.9 billion fiscal stimulus to green investments as well as launching a 'Green economy' budget in April 2009... In February 2009, the USA adopted a US$78.5 billion American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, which included measures to retrofit buildings and expand mass transit, freight rail and renewable energy as well as construct a 'smart' electrical grid transmission system.

significance.justification: Indicates that fiscal policy can embed environmental objectives within broader economic stimulus.
significance.supporting_text: In 2009, some G20 governments adopted policies to boost aggregate demand and growth, which included a sizeable green fiscal component.

concepts.name: GGND recommendation

concepts.supporting_text: ...falling short of the 1 per cent GGND recommendation.

significance.justification: The text notes that actual spending fell short of the 1 % GGND benchmark, highlighting a gap.
significance.supporting_text: falling short of the 1 per cent GGND recommendation.

concepts.name: Environmental pricing policies
concepts.definition: Policy measures that aim to correct market distortions by pricing environmental externalities, for example by reducing fossil‑fuel subsidies and implementing effective environmental taxes or regulations.
concepts.supporting_text: Edward B. Barbier, a consultant on the GGND, has argued that the G20 failed to instigate a worldwide green recovery, and called for further measures to reduce market distortions such as the fossil fuel subsidies and develop effective environmental pricing policies and regulations.

significance.justification: Proposed as a tool to correct market distortions and steer economies toward sustainability.
significance.supporting_text: called for further measures to reduce market distortions such as the fossil fuel subsidies and develop effective environmental pricing policies and regulations.

concepts.name: Low‑carbon, resource‑efficient economy
concepts.definition: An economy that minimizes carbon emissions and uses resources efficiently, thereby reducing dependence on fossil fuels.
concepts.supporting_text: This is the first time there has been a concerted global effort to combine environmental and economic measures to create a low‑carbon, resource‑efficient and less fossil fuel‑dependent economy.

significance.justification: The text frames this economy as the desired outcome of the global green effort, indicating a systemic shift.
significance.supporting_text: first time there has been a concerted global effort ... to create a low‑carbon, resource‑efficient and less fossil fuel‑dependent economy

concepts.name: Environmentally perverse subsidies
concepts.definition: Subsidies that damage the environment, such as large fossil‑fuel subsidies, which are described as a gross misallocation of capital.
concepts.supporting_text: Pavan Sukhdev, head of UNEP's green economy work, described existing economic measures, such as the US$600 billion a year spent on global fossil fuel subsidies, as a 'gross misallocation of capital'.

significance.justification: The passage highlights these subsidies as damaging practices that need to be limited.
significance.supporting_text: limiting spending on environmentally perverse subsidies that damage the environment

concepts.name: Decoupling
concepts.definition: The attempt to break the link between economic growth and worsening environmental quality, potentially achieved by reconfiguring production processes and redesigning goods and services so the economy can grow without exceeding ecological limits.
concepts.supporting_text: In response, attempts have been made at 'decoupling' or breaking the link between economic growth and worsening environmental quality. Theoretically this could be achieved by reconfiguring production processes and redesigning goods and services. In doing so, it is hoped that the economy can continue to grow without exceeding ecological limits.

significance.justification: Posits a pathway to separate economic growth from environmental degradation.
significance.supporting_text: attempts have been made at ‘decoupling’ or breaking the link between economic growth and worsening environmental quality.

concepts.name: Intergenerational justice
concepts.definition: A principle within sustainable development that calls for fairness and responsibility toward future generations in the use of ecological resources.
concepts.supporting_text: principles of sustainable development - equity, intergenerational justice and personal responsibility, and improvement of human wellbeing

significance.justification: Highlights a normative dimension essential for long‑term ecological stewardship.
significance.supporting_text: based on principles of sustainable development – equity, intergenerational justice and personal responsibility...

concepts.name: Personal responsibility
concepts.definition: A principle within sustainable development that emphasizes individual accountability for environmental impacts and the wellbeing of future generations.
concepts.supporting_text: principles of sustainable development - equity, intergenerational justice and personal responsibility, and improvement of human wellbeing

significance.justification: Emphasizes individual agency in achieving ecological outcomes.
significance.supporting_text: based on principles of sustainable development – equity, intergenerational justice and personal responsibility...

concepts.name: Consumerism
concepts.definition: The ideology that equates personal fulfillment, social status, and spiritual satisfaction with the acquisition and display of material goods.
concepts.supporting_text: Our enormously productive economy demands that we make consumption our way of life, that we convert the buying and use of goods into rituals, that we seek our spiritual satisfactions, our ego satisfactions, in consumption. The measure of social status, of social acceptance, of prestige, is now to be found in our consumptive patterns.
supporting_texts: Our enormously productive economy demands that we make consumption our way of life, that we convert the buying and use of goods into rituals, that we seek our spiritual satisfactions, our ego satisfactions, in consumption. The measure of social status, of social acceptance, of prestige, is now to be found in our consumptive patterns.

the values and beliefs that underpin the mainstream culture of consumerism that defines twenty-first-century living.

significance.supporting_text: Our enormously productive economy demands that we make consumption our way of life ... the measure of social status ... is now to be found in our consumptive patterns

concepts.name: Post‑war consumer boom
concepts.definition: The rapid increase in production and consumption that followed World War II, driven by economic growth, the Marshall Plan, and a rising baby boom, which contributed to the rise of consumer culture on both sides of the Atlantic.
concepts.supporting_text: The phenomenal expansion in production and consumption contributed to a post‑war baby boom and the rise of consumerism on both sides of the Atlantic.

significance.justification: Marks a historic surge in consumption that reshaped human‑nature relations.
significance.supporting_text: The phenomenal expansion in production and consumption contributed to a post‑war baby boom and the rise of consumerism...

concepts.name: Car culture
concepts.definition: A societal pattern in which personal automobile ownership and use become central to daily life and identity, reflected in massive post‑war increases in car sales and the emergence of motorways.
concepts.supporting_text: By 1950, Americans had embraced the car culture, with new car sales totalling 6.7 million.

significance.supporting_text: By 1950, Americans had embraced the car culture, with new car sales totalling 6.7 million

significance.justification: Represents organized citizen action demanding safer, cleaner products.
significance.supporting_text: Nader’s book ... prompted a new type of consumer advocacy

concepts.name: Consumer culture
concepts.definition: A post‑war social condition in which consumption becomes a way of life, shaping rituals, status, and identity through the acquisition and use of goods.
concepts.supporting_text: Television, together with radio and the press, contributed to the development of a post‑war consumer culture.

significance.justification: Shows how media fostered mass consumption patterns.
significance.supporting_text: Television, together with radio and the press, contributed to the development of a post‑war consumer culture

concepts.name: Affluent Society
concepts.definition: A theoretical framework describing the paradox of rising private wealth alongside growing environmental degradation and social imbalance.
concepts.supporting_text: The economist J. K. Galbraith (1908-2006) eloquently identified the imbalance between the new‑found private wealth and its environmental effects in his book The Affluent Society (1956).

significance.justification: The concept is used to highlight the imbalance between wealth and environmental harm.
significance.supporting_text: Galbraith ... identified the imbalance between the new‑found private wealth and its environmental effects in his book The Affluent Society (1956).

concepts.name: Media‑driven environmental awareness
concepts.definition: The process by which television and other mass‑media outlets raise public consciousness of pollution and ecological crises through coverage of environmental incidents.
concepts.supporting_text: Television was starting to raise public awareness of pollution. Coverage of the 1969 oil slick fire on the Cuyahoga River and the Santa Barbara Channel oil spill were key moments in the growing media coverage of the human impact on the environment.

significance.justification: Media coverage of pollution incidents raised public awareness of environmental issues.
significance.supporting_text: Television was starting to raise public awareness of pollution. Coverage of the 1969 oil slick fire on the Cuyahoga River … were key moments.

concepts.name: Television advertising as a powerful weapon

significance.supporting_text: Victor Lebow acknowledged that television was a ‘powerful weapon’ for producers.

concepts.name: national cleanliness ethic

significance.supporting_text: promote and develop a national cleanliness ethic

significance.supporting_text: iconic symbol of personal environmental responsibility

significance.supporting_text: Woodbury, New Jersey was the first US city to begin materials recovery, spearheaded by an environmentally concerned community organisation.

significance.supporting_text: "Save it" campaign to promote energy conservation.

significance.supporting_text: A boom in ethical investment saw the launch of six new British ethical funds.
